opening: Tutor me on Bayes' theorem, I keep getting it wrong.

turns.text:
Let's fix that properly. Here's how I've split Bayes' theorem into subskills. We'll track each one from 0 to 5:

1. Conditional probability: what P(A|B) actually means
2. Direction: telling P(A|B) apart from P(B|A)
3. Priors and base rates: why the starting probability matters
4. Total probability: building the denominator P(B)
5. Applying Bayes to real problems (medical tests, spam filters, etc.)
6. Sequential updating: using a posterior as the next prior
7. Odds form and likelihood ratios

First I'll ask a few questions, one at a time, to see what you already know. I won't teach anything yet. Answer in your own words, and don't worry about getting things wrong. That's what the diagnostic is for.

Question 1: In plain English, what's the difference between "the probability that someone is a smoker, given they have lung cancer" and "the probability that someone has lung cancer, given they are a smoker"? Would you expect those two numbers to be roughly the same, or very different, and why?
Hmm, I think they're basically the same thing just worded differently? Smoking and lung cancer are strongly linked, so I'd guess both numbers are pretty high and roughly similar.

Got it, noted. I won't tell you yet whether that's right. We're still in the diagnostic, so let's keep going.

Question 2: Imagine a town of 1,000 people. 200 of them are smokers. 10 people in the town have lung cancer, and 8 of those 10 are smokers.

Using just those numbers, what fraction of the people with lung cancer are smokers? And what fraction of the smokers have lung cancer?
Okay, of the 10 people with lung cancer, 8 are smokers, so that's 8 out of 10, about 80%. That feels about what I'd expect given how linked they are.

Noted. You answered the first half. Question 2 also asked a second thing, and I need that before we move on.

Using the same town (1,000 people, 200 smokers, 10 with lung cancer, 8 of whom smoke): what fraction of the smokers have lung cancer?

Oh, so that's 8 smokers with cancer out of 200 smokers total... 8 out of 200 is like 4%? Huh, that's way lower than I expected, but I guess it's because there are so many more smokers than cancer cases.

Noted. I'm keeping my comments on your answers until the diagnostic is done, so on to the next one.

Question 3: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test for it comes back positive for 99% of people who have the disease. It also comes back positive, wrongly, for 5% of people who don't have it.

A randomly chosen person takes the test and it comes back positive. Roughly what's the chance they actually have the disease? Give your best rough number and explain how you got it.
